title: Obstructive Urinary Disease: Hydronephrosis and Renal Calculi
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)

overview.intro: This chapter explains what happens when urine cannot leave the kidney. It covers the causes of hydronephrosis at each age, how back pressure lowers filtration and destroys the papillae and cortex, why one blocked kidney can go unnoticed while two cause acute kidney injury, and why relief can be followed by a large diuresis. It then explains how urine chemistry, especially pH, decides which kidney stone forms, and how a moving stone produces renal colic, obstruction, and infection. Board questions usually give an age, a sex, a urine pH, a crystal, or a radiograph and ask for the cause, stone type, or complication, so each topic is taught from the mechanism outward.

sections.title: Causes of hydronephrosis and how obstruction destroys the kidney

blocks.text: Hydronephrosis is dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces; when caused by obstruction it brings progressive parenchymal atrophy. A block at or below the bladder neck dilates both upper tracts, while a block at the ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) or along one ureter dilates only the kidney above it. Vesicoureteral reflux and pregnancy also widen the collecting system without true obstruction.

blocks.text: Why back pressure lowers GFR

Filtration continues when outflow is blocked; filtrate escapes into the interstitium, lymphatics, and veins, so the pelvis keeps distending. Pressure is transmitted back through the collecting ducts to Bowman space. Because GFR equals Kf multiplied by (glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure minus Bowman space pressure minus glomerular oncotic pressure), every rise in Bowman space pressure subtracts directly from net filtration pressure.

The kidney first defends filtration with prostaglandin and nitric oxide mediated afferent dilation. Within hours angiotensin II and thromboxane constrict preglomerular vessels, so renal blood flow and GFR fall together. Persisting obstruction recruits macrophages, and angiotensin II and TGF-beta drive tubular apoptosis and interstitial fibrosis.

blocks.title: Worked example: a small pressure change, a large GFR change
blocks.text: Using about 60 mmHg glomerular capillary pressure, 18 mmHg Bowman space pressure, and 32 mmHg mean oncotic pressure, net filtration pressure is 60 minus 18 minus 32, or 10 mmHg. If obstruction raises Bowman space pressure to 25 mmHg, net pressure falls to 3 mmHg, and with Kf unchanged that kidney's GFR falls by about 70% although its glomeruli are normal. Afferent dilation raising glomerular pressure to 65 mmHg restores net pressure only to 8 mmHg. Net filtration pressure is a small difference between large forces, so modest back pressure has a large effect.
Papillary and cortical atrophy

Injury begins in the medulla. The papillae project into the calyces and take the full pelvic pressure, and the distended pelvis compresses the low-pressure vasa recta. Papillary ischemia comes first, so the earliest loss is tubular: urine cannot be concentrated, and distal H+ and K+ secretion fails, sometimes causing hyperkalemic distal renal tubular acidosis. Calyces lose their cupped papillary impressions and become blunted. Cortical tubules then atrophy and are replaced by fibrosis while glomeruli survive until late, leaving dilated calyces within a thin cortical rim. Partial or intermittent obstruction produces the largest kidneys because filtration continues long enough to distend the system. Function largely recovers if complete obstruction is relieved within about 1 to 2 weeks, and little returns after several weeks.

sections.title: Unilateral versus bilateral obstruction and postobstructive diuresis

blocks.text: Serum creatinine reflects total GFR from both kidneys. When one kidney is obstructed, the other raises its single-nephron GFR, so total GFR falls by much less than half and creatinine stays normal or rises only slightly. A congenital UPJ obstruction or a slowly growing pelvic tumor can therefore destroy one kidney silently and be found only on imaging, or present with infection, hematuria, or hypertension. An acute stone hurts because of sudden distension, not because of lost function.

Bilateral obstruction, obstruction of a solitary functioning kidney, or a block at the bladder outlet removes all filtration reserve and causes postrenal acute kidney injury (AKI). Complete obstruction produces anuria. Partial obstruction may produce oliguria, or a normal or even high output of dilute urine because the injured medulla cannot concentrate; output alternating between anuria and polyuria suggests intermittent obstruction. Urea and creatinine rise, and failed distal secretion causes hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis. Early on, slow tubular flow increases urea reabsorption, so the BUN to creatinine ratio may exceed about 15 to 20 and the urine can resemble prerenal urine; as tubules are damaged, sodium excretion rises and urine osmolality approaches that of plasma. A distended bladder points to a block below the bladder neck.

blocks.text: Postobstructive diuresis

After bilateral obstruction is relieved, urine output can exceed about 200 mL/h for several hours or about 3 L per day. Part of this diuresis is appropriate: urea, sodium, and water retained during obstruction are excreted, and the retained urea acts as an osmotic diuretic. Part reflects tubular injury: collecting duct cells have downregulated aquaporin-2 and respond poorly to ADH, sodium transporters along the nephron are reduced, the medullary solute gradient has washed out, and natriuretic peptides released during volume expansion keep promoting sodium loss. The result can be volume depletion, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and either hyponatremia or hypernatremia depending on free water loss. Once the retained load is cleared, a healthy kidney ends the diuresis; an injured one may keep wasting salt and water.

blocks.title: Mechanism of postobstructive diuresis
steps: Bilateral obstruction relieved
Retained urea is filtered and drives osmotic diuresis
Low aquaporin-2: poor response to ADH
Fewer Na+ transporters; medullary gradient washed out
Large volume of dilute urine rich in Na+ and K+
Risk of volume depletion, hypokalemia, and sodium disorders
blocks.caption: Appropriate excretion of retained solute and true tubular dysfunction combine after relief.

blocks.predict: A 74-year-old man with prostatic enlargement has a bladder palpable to the umbilicus, creatinine 5.8 mg/dL, and potassium 6.1 mmol/L. After the bladder is drained, what happens to his urine output and serum potassium over the next day?
blocks.explain: Output rises sharply as retained urea causes osmotic diuresis and injured collecting ducts ignore ADH. Potassium falls as distal flow and K+ excretion increase, and can overshoot into hypokalemia.

sections.title: Kidney stones classified by composition and urine pH

blocks.text: A stone forms when urine is supersaturated with a salt, so crystals nucleate, grow, and aggregate faster than flow clears them. Supersaturation rises with high excretion of the solute, low urine volume, and a urine pH that lowers solubility. Inhibitors oppose this: citrate binds calcium in a soluble complex, and proteins such as uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein) block aggregation. Chronic acidosis increases proximal citrate reabsorption, and the resulting hypocitraturia removes a key inhibitor. Many calcium oxalate stones grow on Randall plaques, papillary calcium phosphate deposits that erode through the urothelium.

Urine pH organizes the classification. Phosphate is less soluble as pH rises, because more of it exists as HPO4 2- and PO4 3-, so calcium phosphate and struvite need alkaline urine. Uric acid (pKa about 5.5) is mainly the poorly soluble undissociated acid below that pH, so uric acid stones need acidic urine. Cystine also precipitates in acidic urine and dissolves well only above a pH of about 7.5. Calcium oxalate solubility barely changes with pH.

blocks.title: Kidney stone types
rows: Calcium oxalate (most common; calcium stones about 75 to 80%)
Hypercalciuria, enteric hyperoxaluria, ethylene glycol, hypocitraturia
Urease producers: Proteus, Klebsiella, Staphylococcus saprophyticus
Gout, tumor lysis, insulin resistance, chronic diarrhea
blocks.caption: Phosphate stones need alkaline urine, uric acid and cystine acidic urine; calcium oxalate forms at any pH.

blocks.text: Most calcium stone formers have idiopathic hypercalciuria with a normal serum calcium. In primary hyperparathyroidism the filtered calcium load rises so much that urinary calcium increases despite PTH-driven distal reabsorption. In ileal disease, unabsorbed fatty acids bind dietary calcium, leaving oxalate free for colonic absorption, and ethylene glycol is metabolized to oxalate. Distal renal tubular acidosis favors calcium phosphate through alkaline urine, hypercalciuria from bone buffering, and hypocitraturia.

Struvite forms only with infection by urease producers (flow below); E. coli, the commonest urinary pathogen, generally lacks urease. Uric acid stones contain no calcium, so they are radiolucent on plain films; persistently acidic urine is the dominant cause, and tumor lysis or high urate excretion in gout adds solute. Cystinuria is a defect of the apical transporter for cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine in the proximal tubule and gut; only cystine, the least soluble, forms stones. Stones begin young, recur, and show hexagonal crystals and a positive cyanide-nitroprusside test.

blocks.title: How urease produces a struvite staghorn
steps: Urease-producing bacteria infect the urine
Urease splits urea into NH3 and CO2
NH3 binds H+ to form NH4+; urine pH rises
Mg2+, NH4+, and phosphate precipitate as struvite
Stone grows around surviving bacteria into a staghorn
blocks.caption: Infection creates the chemistry, and the stone shelters the infection.

blocks.title: Worked example: reasoning from radiograph and pH
blocks.text: A 52-year-old man with gout has renal colic. A plain radiograph shows no stone, noncontrast CT shows a 6 mm ureteral stone, and urine pH is 5.0. A stone invisible on plain film lacks calcium, excluding calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate, and struvite. Cystine is faintly radiopaque. At pH 5.0 uric acid is in its poorly soluble form, so the stone is uric acid. By contrast, recurrent infection, urine pH 8.0, coffin-lid crystals, and a branched radiopaque stone indicate struvite.

blocks.predict: A child with distal renal tubular acidosis and an adult with cystinuria both form stones. Which stone does each form, and at what urine pH?
blocks.explain: Distal RTA cannot acidify urine and causes hypercalciuria and hypocitraturia: calcium phosphate in alkaline urine. Cystine is least soluble in acidic urine, so cystine stones form at low pH.
blocks.check: Compare with the pH paragraph and stone table.

sections.title: Renal colic and the complications of calculi

blocks.text: Renal colic is pain from acute obstruction of the upper urinary tract, usually a stone moving from the pelvis into the ureter. Sudden distension of the ureter, pelvis, and renal capsule stimulates stretch receptors, and ureteral smooth muscle contracts harder against the stone, while local prostaglandins sensitize nerve endings. Despite the name, the pain is often a steady severe ache with waves of exacerbation as peristalsis pushes against the obstruction. The patient typically cannot lie still, unlike a patient with peritonitis, who stays motionless.

Visceral afferents from the kidney and ureter travel with sympathetic fibers to roughly the T11 to L2 spinal segments, so pain is referred to the skin of those segments. A high stone causes flank and loin pain; as it descends, pain moves to the lower abdomen and groin and into the ipsilateral testis or labium majus. A stone at the ureterovesical junction irritates the bladder, adding urgency, frequency, and dysuria, sometimes with pain at the tip of the penis. Nausea and vomiting reflect shared autonomic pathways through the celiac and renal plexuses. Hematuria, gross or microscopic, comes from mucosal abrasion and is present in most but not all patients, so its absence does not exclude a stone.

rows: Where the funnel-shaped pelvis joins the ureter
Where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels near the common iliac bifurcation
Lower abdomen radiating to the groin
Oblique passage through the bladder wall; narrowest point
Groin, scrotum or labium, with urgency and dysuria
blocks.caption: Stones stop where the lumen narrows; the ureterovesical junction is the most common site of impaction.

blocks.text: Complications

A stone that blocks the ureter produces acute hydronephrosis above it, with the pressure effects described in C01. Small stones usually pass, but the chance falls as size increases, and stones larger than about 5 to 10 mm often remain impacted. Persistent impaction destroys that kidney progressively, often silently once the pain settles, because the other kidney maintains the creatinine.

Infection above a stone is the most dangerous complication. Normal urine flow flushes bacteria out; stagnant urine above an obstruction lets them multiply, and raised pelvic pressure pushes bacteria and endotoxin into the renal veins and lymphatics. The infected obstructed system can become pyonephrosis, a perinephric abscess, or urosepsis, so fever with an obstructing stone signals a life-threatening infection. Struvite stones harbor bacteria inside them, so the infection persists while the stone remains. Long-standing staghorn calculi with chronic Proteus infection are associated with xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, and chronic irritation can cause squamous metaplasia and, rarely, squamous cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis.

blocks.title: Stone, stasis, and infection
steps: Stone narrows the outflow
Urine stagnates above the stone
Bacteria multiply instead of being flushed out
Urease organisms alkalinize urine; struvite precipitates
Stone enlarges and obstruction worsens
blocks.caption: With urease-producing organisms, obstruction and infection reinforce each other until the stone becomes a staghorn.

blocks.predict: Two patients have the same 7 mm stone at the ureterovesical junction. One is afebrile; the other has a temperature of 39.2 °C (102.6 °F). Why is the second patient in much greater danger?
blocks.explain: Trapped urine cannot clear bacteria, and high pelvic pressure drives organisms into the bloodstream, so an infected obstructed kidney can progress to pyonephrosis and urosepsis within hours.

integration.text: Anatomy explains where and in whom obstruction occurs: the male urethra and prostate, the right ureter at the pelvic brim in pregnancy, the three ureteral narrowings, and the T11 to L2 referral of ureteral pain. Physiology explains the damage: Bowman space pressure subtracts from filtration, the vasa recta and papillae fail first, and creatinine reflects both kidneys together. Biochemistry and microbiology explain stone type: solubility depends on pH, purine breakdown supplies uric acid, ethylene glycol supplies oxalate, a single transporter defect causes cystinuria, and bacterial urease converts urea into the alkaline chemistry of struvite. Pathology ties these together as blunted calyces, a thin cortical rim, and staghorn stones with chronic infection.

These patterns have limits. Dilation is not proof of obstruction, because reflux and pregnancy widen the collecting system without destroying it, and severe early obstruction can cause little dilation. A normal creatinine does not exclude obstruction of one kidney. Many stones are mixed, so a calcium oxalate stone may carry calcium phosphate, and a plain radiograph that misses a uric acid stone does not mean no stone is present.

summary: Hydronephrosis is dilation of the pelvis and calyces; obstruction adds progressive atrophy of the parenchyma.

Posterior urethral valves (newborn boys), UPJ obstruction (congenital), stones (young adults), pregnancy (right more than left), prostatic enlargement (older men), and pelvic tumors (women) are the classic causes.
Back pressure raises Bowman space pressure and lowers net filtration pressure; later angiotensin II and thromboxane cut renal blood flow.
Papillae and vasa recta fail first, so a concentrating defect precedes cortical thinning; partial obstruction causes the most dilation.
Unilateral obstruction can stay silent because the other kidney keeps creatinine normal; bilateral or outlet obstruction causes postrenal AKI with oliguria or anuria, hyperkalemia, and acidosis.
Postobstructive diuresis combines osmotic diuresis from retained urea with ADH resistance and sodium wasting from injured tubules.
Calcium oxalate is the most common stone and forms at any pH; calcium phosphate and struvite need alkaline urine; uric acid and cystine need acidic urine.
Urease splits urea to ammonia, alkalinizing urine and precipitating struvite staghorns that shelter bacteria.
Uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain films; cystine stones show hexagonal crystals.

Renal colic is steady severe pain with waves, radiating from flank to groin with hematuria; stones lodge at the UPJ, pelvic brim, and ureterovesical junction, and infection above a stone can cause urosepsis.

verify: Stone composition percentages differ between sources (calcium stones about 70 to 80%, struvite about 10 to 15%, uric acid about 5 to 10%, cystine about 1 to 2%); confirm the figures NABNE expects.
Spinal segments for ureteral pain are given as T11 to L2 in Moore and as T10 to L2 or T10 to L1 in other texts.
Timing of recovery after complete obstruction (about 1 to 2 weeks for near-full recovery) comes largely from animal studies and is quoted differently across sources.
The definition of postobstructive diuresis (more than about 200 mL/h for several hours or more than about 3 L per day) is a clinical convention that varies between references.
Urine pH thresholds for struvite precipitation (about 7.2) and cystine solubility (about 7.5) are approximate and vary slightly by source.
The BUN to creatinine ratio cutoff for early postrenal AKI is quoted as greater than 15 or greater than 20 in different texts.
The proportion of renal colic presenting with hematuria (often quoted near 85%) varies between series; the chapter states only that most patients have it.
Confirm whether NABNE expects Randall plaques, Potter sequence, and xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis by name.
